clue.text: Critic's starting on Affleck war film: 'Terrible piece of costume'

indicators.note: a word's starting point is its opening letter, so only the head of the critic is wanted

blocks.note: the opening letter of the critic
Ben Affleck directed and starred in Argo, about the Iran hostage crisis
British slang: something pants is rubbish or terrible

explanation.surface: A critic opens a review of an Affleck war film by sneering at one of the outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Terrible piece of costume' look like the critic's verdict, but 'Terrible' is wordplay and only 'piece of costume' defines. Cargo pants are trousers with big side pockets.
explanation.definitionFit: Trousers with large pocketed thighs are an item of clothing, which an actor's wardrobe would call one item of their outfit.

clue.text: Salesman might travel with this suit

blocks.note: first meaning: a travelling salesman carries his samples in a bag of this kind
second meaning: a lawsuit, an action brought in court

explanation.surface: A travelling salesman packs the suit he will wear on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' looks like the clothes the salesman takes along; it is a legal action.
explanation.definitionFit: A sample case is luggage carried by reps, and a court case is a legal proceeding, which is what a lawsuit means.

clue.text: A shower are in charge, we're informed

indicators.note: being informed suggests being told by word of mouth, so the sound of the phrase matters, not its spelling

blocks.note: those who are in charge reign, which sounds identical to a word for falling water

explanation.surface: A gossipy note that some group is now running things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A shower' looks like slang for a useless bunch who are in charge; it is the definition, a spell of wet weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief fall of water drops from clouds is a light spell of precipitation of this very kind.

clue.text: Cocky, losing head, leaders of Tranmere Rovers find cash for 75,000-capacity ground

indicators.note: to lose one's head here is to lose the first letter, so the word for cocky is cut at the front
the leaders of a group of words are their opening letters

blocks.note: cocky means bold, brash
the initial letters of the football club's name
to afford something is to be able to find the money for it

explanation.surface: Cocky Tranmere Rovers, a lower-league football club, try to raise money for a huge stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: BOLD loses its B to give OLD. Tranmere Rovers is a small club near Liverpool, which fits the football picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Trafford is Manchester United's football stadium, which holds roughly seventy-five thousand spectators.

clue.text: Puts up with ridiculous spectacle endlessly ... and again

indicators.note: something ridiculous is absurdly out of order, so the remaining letters are jumbled
endlessly removes the final letter, and 'and again' repeats that cut a second time

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tolerates a ridiculous show that seems to go on endlessly, over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: SPECTACLE loses its last letter twice, E then L, leaving SPECTAC to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To tolerate or put up with something is to take it on board without objecting, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Pair of moody teenagers with pained expression: time to get up

indicators.note: in a down clue, to get up is to travel upwards, so the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: emos are gloomy young fans of emo music
a cry of pain
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Two sulky teenagers groan when told it is time to get out of bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple of people taken together form a duo, a set of two.

clue.text: Took ideas from some flipping trade paperback

indicators.note: some of the words means only part of them is used, a run of letters inside them
flipping something turns it over, so the run of letters is read backwards

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A writer is accused of plagiarising a cheap paperback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads like a mild British curse on the paperback, but it reverses the hidden letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape is to imitate or mimic, which is what copying someone else's ideas amounts to.

clue.text: Fat Paisley comic? Don't take chances

indicators.note: a comic version of something is a farcical mangling of it, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A heavy comedian named Paisley advised to stay cautious.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to act cautiously and avoid risk, the same as refusing to gamble.

clue.text: Weakened, foolish Everyman, regularly unfit, dropped

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is kept

blocks.note: dim means stupid
the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I
the second and fourth letters
to shed is to drop or cast off

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to being worn out, silly and out of shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Something diminished has been reduced or made smaller, so it is lessened in strength.

clue.text: (n.) I do PR; cost is ludicrous

definitions.text: (n.) I do PR; cost is ludicrous

indicators.note: ludicrous means absurd and senseless, signalling that the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, the abbreviation for noun
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style entry for a publicist who admits their fees are absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: The '(n.)' looks like dictionary labelling of a noun, but its N is part of the letters to rearrange; read whole, the clue is the spin doctor speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin doctor is a press officer who presents news favourably, so public relations is their trade and they are expensive.

clue.text: Regularly tweak rump that's kind of hot

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Someone keeps pinching a backside to make it glow.
explanation.definitionFit: Warmth is a mild degree of heat, so being warm is a gentle level of hotness.

clue.text: Corn, potato and grain regularly moving?

definitions.text: Corn, potato and grain regularly moving?

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is kept
moving things shifts their positions, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: Farm crops being moved round in a regular cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the farming practice itself, with the question mark admitting the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmers grow different plants in a field in a set sequence each year, so the crops move around regularly.

clue.text: Ice can coat river flowing into this!

definitions.text: Ice can coat river flowing into this!

indicators.note: flowing water churns and moves, so the letters before it are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A frozen sea where ice may coat the rivers that run into it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the polar sea, frozen over with rivers draining into it; the exclamation mark flags the double reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The northernmost ocean is largely ice-covered and fed by great Siberian and Canadian rivers.

clue.text: Landlord in favour of clergyman being denied special old rum, to begin with

indicators.note: being denied something means going without it, so a letter is taken out of the clergyman
what comes to begin with in each word is its opening letter

blocks.note: pro means for, in favour of
a priest is a member of the clergy
S is the abbreviation for special; it is the letter removed
the initial letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A pub landlord takes the side of a vicar refused a special old rum at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: PRIEST loses its S to give PRIET.
explanation.definitionFit: A proprietor is an owner, and a landlord owns the property or pub he lets or runs.

clue.text: Uncommonly able-bodied seaman? No: Royal Marine and partner in war

blocks.note: AB is the abbreviation for an able-bodied seaman
taken as written
RM is the abbreviation for Royal Marine
an ally is a nation fighting on the same side

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a strong sailor is unusual, and is told it is a marine and his comrade instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Able-bodied seaman?' seems to question whether the sailor is fit; the abbreviation AB is standard for a rated sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something abnormally means doing it in an unusual way, the same as uncommonly.

clue.text: Live regressively, wearing Elizabethan garb, getting expressions of disrespect

indicators.note: moving regressively means going backwards, so the word for live is read from its end
something wearing clothes sits inside them, so these letters go within the garb

blocks.note: ruffs are the stiff pleated collars worn in Elizabeth I's time
to be is to live, exist

explanation.surface: Living in the past by dressing in Tudor costume earns someone snubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebuffs are snubs or curt refusals, which show a lack of respect for the person rejected.

clue.text: Forgives cuts wherein university ousts Italian

indicators.note: to oust someone is to push them out and take their place, so one letter replaces another

blocks.note: to excise is to cut out
U is the abbreviation for university
I is the abbreviation for Italian

explanation.surface: A university accepts spending cuts that drive out its Italian staff.
explanation.walkthrough: In EXCISES the I is replaced by U.
explanation.definitionFit: To excuse someone is to pardon or let them off, which is what a person who forgives does.

clue.text: Tire out, made to include 'exciting' meeting with press

indicators.note: something made to include another thing has it put inside, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: to poop is informal for to exhaust, as in pooped
hot means exciting, sensational

explanation.surface: A tiring press event that is supposed to be exciting.
explanation.walkthrough: Being pooped is informal, chiefly American, for being worn out.
explanation.definitionFit: A photo op is a staged chance for journalists and photographers to picture a public figure.

clue.text: Primarily, practically, your really resolute hardship is counter-productive?

definitions.text: Primarily, practically, your really resolute hardship is counter-productive?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the initial letter of each following word is used

blocks.clueFragment: practically, your really resolute hardship is counter-productive
blocks.note: the initial letters of the seven words

explanation.surface: A warning that dogged endurance of hardship may end up doing you more harm than good.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue defines a victory won at such cost it defeats itself, named after King Pyrrhus.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pyrrhic victory costs the winner so much that it is in effect a defeat, so the effort backfires.

clue.text: Inhale a little nasty smell, tucking into starter of snails with the French

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its opening letter
tucking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes within the others

blocks.note: the first letter
niff is British slang for a bad smell
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A diner catches a whiff of something unpleasant while eating escargots in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into' and 'starter' set a dinner-table scene, but they are instructions for placing and picking letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To sniffle is to draw air in through the nose in small repeated breaths, as with a cold.

clue.text: Drunk receiving present delivers rude expression

blocks.note: a sot is a habitual drunk
present means here, in attendance

explanation.surface: A drunk handed a gift answers with a rude remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift; it means in attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a childish retort of defiance, said to have the last word, so it is an impolite exclamation.

clue.text: During mass, lecture describing Dutch and English puritans' approach to pleasure

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so the lecture surrounds the following letters

blocks.note: in means during, as in 'in the night'
M is the abbreviation for mass
an oration is a formal speech
D is the abbreviation for Dutch
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A sermon at church describes how Dutch and English Puritans viewed enjoyment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' and 'puritans' set a church scene, but mass is just the physics abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Puritans allow enjoyment only within strict limits, never to excess, which is what restraint in indulgence means.

clue.text: Essentially meddlesome: drink rejected in book of Bible

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so its central letters are kept
something rejected is sent back, so the letters so far are read in reverse

blocks.note: the two central letters of a ten-letter word
OJ is the American abbreviation for orange juice

explanation.surface: An interfering person has their drink sent back while studying scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: LE and OJ are joined and the whole of LEOJ is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Joel is one of the twelve minor prophets, and a short book of the Old Testament bears his name.

clue.text: Uncertain moment, scratching head

indicators.note: scratching out the head of a word deletes its first letter

blocks.note: a jiffy is a moment, as in 'back in a jiffy'

explanation.surface: Someone scratches their head, unsure, for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: JIFFY loses its J. Scratching your head is what you do when unsure, which hides the deletion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Iffy is informal for doubtful or dubious, full of ifs.

clue.text: Swiss legend that helps you beat poker rivals

definitions.text: that helps you beat poker rivals

blocks.note: first meaning: William, the Swiss folk hero who shot an apple off his son's head

blocks.clueFragment: that helps you beat poker rivals
blocks.note: second meaning: an unconscious habit that gives away a card player's hand

explanation.surface: A Swiss legend shares a trick for beating opponents at poker.
explanation.definitionFit: William Tell is the archer of Swiss folklore, and in card games a tell is a giveaway gesture opponents can read.

clue.text: Perhaps a little blue shed makes you disgruntled

blocks.note: a piece of blue such as Stilton is one example of this dairy food
to doff is to take off or shed a garment or hat

explanation.surface: A small blue garden shed puts someone in a bad mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue shed' looks like a painted hut; blue is a kind of cheese and shed is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheesed off is British slang for fed up or annoyed, a mood of discontent.

clue.text: Noisily erect beams

indicators.note: noisily points to how a word is spoken out loud rather than written

blocks.note: to erect something is to raise it up

explanation.surface: Builders loudly put up girders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beams' looks like building timbers to be erected; it means shafts of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Shafts of light from the sun or a torch are narrow streams of radiation.

clue.text: Part of film where Rock Hudson finally gets trifle

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word it follows

blocks.note: scree is loose broken rock on a mountainside
the final letter
to trifle or play with something is to toy with it

explanation.surface: A film scene in which the actor Rock Hudson is served a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: Rock Hudson reads as the Hollywood star, but the two words are split. A trifle is a British layered dessert of sponge, custard and cream, which feeds the false picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The script of a film, with dialogue and directions, is one component that goes into making a movie.
